name: Cosmopolitanism
summary: Cosmopolitanism holds that all human beings belong to a single moral community, so that national, ethnic or cultural membership does not limit a person's basic moral standing. Its strands range from moral duties of aid and justice that cross borders, to legal and political proposals for global institutions, to a cultural ideal of valuing diversity and exchange. Most adherents favour reformed global governance or a federation of states rather than a world state, and many accept some limited special loyalties.
scope: Cosmopolitanism as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy defines it: the idea that all human beings are, or can and should be, citizens of a single community, moral, political, cultural or economic. Kant's Perpetual Peace (1795), which the SEP treats as its founding political text, supplies the primary source. The Marxist and economic-liberal strands count only where they split the answer, and the ethnic 'rootless cosmopolitan' smear is excluded. The tradition says little on most domestic economic, social and cultural questions, so those stay null.

sources.title: Cosmopolitanism
sources.author: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Kleingeld and Brown)
sources.usedFor: Defining source: moral, political, cultural and economic cosmopolitanism and their positions on sovereignty, aid, nationalism, trade and courts.

sources.title: Perpetual Peace: A Philosophical Essay (trans. M. Campbell Smith)
sources.author: Immanuel Kant
sources.usedFor: Preliminary and definitive articles: no annexation, abolition of standing armies, non-interference, republican constitution, hospitality and criticism of colonial conduct.

sources.title: Global Justice
sources.author: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.usedFor: Section 2.3 on contemporary cosmopolitans: equal moral worth and equal consideration of interests, and Pogge's impartiality over global rules.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The SEP says the equality of rank of all humans precluded 'feudal hierarchy' (s1).

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Kant's preliminary article forbids any state to 'violently interfere with the constitution and administration of another', and he adds that the erring state 'can much more serve as a warning' (s3).

arms-reduction.rationale: Kant's preliminary article: 'Standing armies shall be abolished in course of time', since they spur states to outrival one another in the number of soldiers; he excepts voluntary periodical military exercises by citizens for defence (s3).

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: The SEP says the cosmopolitan 'encourages cultural diversity and appreciates a multicultural mélange' and rejects exclusive attachment to one culture (s1).

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: The SEP says the fundamental equality of all humans precluded 'tutelage of various sorts' (s1).

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The SEP says the equality of rank of all humans 'precluded slavery, colonial exploitation, feudal hierarchy, and tutelage of various sorts' (s1), and Kant describes the conduct of commercial states toward colonised lands as an injustice 'such as to fill us with horror' (s3).

consent-of-governed.rationale: Kant argues that annexing a state contradicts 'the idea of the original contract without which no right over a people is thinkable' (s3).

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The SEP records a split among political cosmopolitans: Kant held that the league of states should not have coercive military powers, since that would violate internal sovereignty, while others argued a federation with coercive powers is the only way out of the state of nature (s1).

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The SEP says cosmopolitan values have been invoked to oppose slavery and apartheid and to advocate the emancipation of women (s1), and that every human is entitled to equal consideration of interests whatever their national affiliation (s4).

free-trade.rationale: The SEP records economic cosmopolitans (Hayek, Friedman, Hegewisch) favouring free trade for everyone's benefit, while many philosophical cosmopolitans regard a fully globalised market as a partial cause of international inequality (s1).

international-criminal-courts.rationale: The SEP presents the International Criminal Court as an innovative form of cosmopolitanism under which individuals 'can be held responsible for crimes under international law in ways that cut through the shield of state sovereignty' (s1).

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Kant's preliminary article: 'No state shall violently interfere with the constitution and administration of another' (s3), and the SEP reports he requires states to respect each other's internal sovereignty (s1).

nation-first.rationale: The SEP says the cosmopolitan 'rejects a strong nationalism' (s1), and Pogge holds that those designing global rules 'ought to disregard their private and local, including national, commitments and loyalties' (s4); moderates still allow special duties to compatriots.

national-self-determination.rationale: The SEP says the cosmopolitan position rebuffs 'the right to unconditional national self-determination' (s1).

person-over-state.rationale: The SEP reports that cosmopolitans want a theory addressing the needs of individuals directly rather than through states, and criticise institutions that 'entrench state interests at the expense of individuals' (s1); Kant says hiring men to kill 'seems to imply a use of them as mere machines and instruments in the hand of another (namely, the state)' (s3).

pool-sovereignty.rationale: The SEP reports that some cosmopolitans argued states ought to transfer part of their sovereignty to a federal level and that others favour layered or vertically dispersed sovereignty, while Kant's league is voluntary (s1); the strands differ on how far to pool it.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The SEP says cosmopolitan values have been invoked to oppose slavery and apartheid (s1).

revolution-legitimate.rationale: The SEP reports that Marx and later Marxists expected capitalism to provoke a world-wide revolution, a cosmopolitanism of its own (s1), while Kant holds that revolution against even a tyrant is "in the highest degree wrong of the subjects" (s3): the strands split.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: The SEP reports that moral cosmopolitans insist on a duty to aid foreigners who are starving or suffering, whatever their citizenship; strict and moderate cosmopolitans differ only on extra duties to compatriots (s1).

separated-powers.rationale: Kant: 'Republicanism is the political principle of severing the executive power of the government from the legislature', and every non-representative form is 'no true constitution at all' (s3); the SEP reports that Kant requires states to be organised on republican principles (s1).

state-harmful.rationale: The SEP records the debate among cosmopolitans over whether states are 'indispensable instruments in the pursuit of justice' or 'inimical to it', alongside Cloots' call to abolish all states and Kant's and Rawls's league of states (s1).

territorial-expansion.rationale: Kant's preliminary article: no state 'shall be acquired by another through inheritance, exchange, purchase or donation', and he judges the view that a state's glory lies in the unceasing growth of its power scholastic and pedantic (s3).

universal-morality.rationale: The SEP reports Kant's view that all rational beings are members of a single moral community under common laws of morality grounded in reason (s1), and that cosmopolitans hold every human being to be an ultimate unit of moral concern with equal moral worth (s4).

notes: Strands diverge on a world state (Cloots, Cabrera for; Kant, Rawls against), on strict versus moderate special duties to compatriots, and on market versus egalitarian economics. This pass rebuilt the answers on three texts: the SEP Cosmopolitanism entry, Kant's Perpetual Peace and the SEP Global Justice entry (SEP Kant, SEP Stoicism, Cicero's De Officiis and the Communist Manifesto were read and added nothing citable). Themes searched: moral scope, aid, courts and international bodies, sovereignty, nationalism and self-determination, culture and immigration, trade and economics, war and armies, colonialism, constitutional form, hierarchy and equality. Every answer the first pass deduced from general values (domestic economy, religion, gender, crime, environment, party and revolutionary questions) is now null: the sources record no position on it. Kant's own democracy, religion and gender views are not the ideology's position, so they are not used. Kant's separation of powers and consent argument rest on Perpetual Peace alone; the SEP confirms only the republican requirement.
